name: Epicurus
major_ideas: Pleasure as the sole good (Epicurean hedonism)
Freedom from fear of the gods and of death
Epicurean friendship and its tension with egoistic hedonism
biography: A later follower of Democritus who adopted the view that atoms were originally falling under weight, with heavier atoms overtaking lighter ones, a view Russell judges 'rather unintelligent' compared to the random-motion interpretation he favors for Leucippus and Democritus. Founder of the school; held that pleasure is the sole good, but -- distinguishing 'dynamic' from 'static' pleasure -- concluded that the wise life aims at freedom from pain and disturbance (ataraxia) rather than active gratification; built a materialist physics (atoms plus an indeterminate 'swerve') designed above all to remove fear of the gods and of death; taught with dogmatic authority that his followers were not permitted to question.
central_doctrines: Pleasure as the sole good (Epicurean hedonism): The ethical doctrine that pleasure is the beginning and end of the good life, and that virtue, justice, wisdom, and culture have value only insofar as they serve or are 'referred to' the pursuit of pleasure and the avoidance of pain. Dynamic versus static pleasure: 'Dynamic' (or active) pleasures are those attained through the process of satisfying a prior desire that was accompanied by pain; 'static' pleasures consist in a state of painless equilibrium that results simply from the absence of unsatisfied desire, requiring no painful stimulus beforehand. Materialist physics with the atomic 'swerve': Epicurus's physical theory that the world consists of falling atoms and void; atoms, which fall downward in an absolute (not merely earth-directed) sense, occasionally undergo a slight, uncaused 'swerve' from their straight path, producing collisions and (Epicurus hoped) making room for undetermined human choice within an otherwise mechanistic universe. Freedom from fear of the gods and of death: Epicurus's core therapeutic goal: to remove the two chief sources of human anxiety by philosophical argument -- first, by holding that the gods, though real, do not interfere in or punish human affairs, and second, by holding that the soul is material and dissolves at death, so that the dead have no sensation and therefore cannot suffer.
key_arguments: Argument that death is 'nothing to us'
Argument for the superiority of static over dynamic pleasure

disagreements.about: Pleasure as the sole good (Epicurean hedonism)
Freedom from fear of the gods and of death

russell_view: Russell presents Epicurus with considerable personal sympathy, taking pains to defend him against Stoic-originated scandal (e.g. about his mother, or about debauchery in the Garden) as unreliable, malicious gossip. He stresses the coherence and sincerity of Epicurus's system: it is a genuinely therapeutic philosophy, aimed entirely at securing tranquility by removing the two great sources of Hellenistic fear (the gods and death), and Russell credits Epicurus with real intellectual consistency in following hedonism to its most austere conclusions rather than its most self-indulgent ones. At the same time, Russell is critical of Epicurus's intellectual narrowness: contempt for predecessors, dogmatic insistence that followers not deviate from his teaching, indifference to mathematics and logic, and a lack of genuine curiosity about which of several possible naturalistic explanations of a phenomenon (e.g. lunar phases) is actually true, since for Epicurus any non-religious explanation serves the therapeutic purpose equally well. Russell judges this incuriosity to be why the Epicureans 'contributed practically nothing to natural knowledge' despite their materialism. He treats Lucretius's poem as the vehicle through which Epicureanism became known to the modern world, emphasizes the striking historical irony that professedly anti-religious, materialist doctrines are presented by Lucretius with quasi-religious fervor, and closes by tracing Epicureanism's decline (in favor of Stoicism, then Neoplatonism among philosophers, and Christianity among the masses) and its distant revival by Bentham and the French philosophes.
why_this_matters: Epicurus held that pleasure is the sole good, but distinguished 'dynamic' (active) from 'static' (equilibrium) pleasure and concluded the wise life aims at static pleasure -- freedom from pain and disturbance -- rather than intense gratification. Epicurus adopted Democritus's atomism but added the unpredictable atomic 'swerve' so that his fully materialist physics would still leave room for human free will.
